lessons.title: Opening a Second Location or Franchising
lessons.body: Before opening a second location, ensure your first salon runs without you daily. Track monthly profit for at least 6 months. If net profit is consistently above 20% of revenue, you are ready. In Nairobi, a small salon with 4 chairs can net KES 150,000 monthly. To open a second, you need 6 months of operating costs saved: rent, salaries, supplies. For a similar salon, budget KES 800,000 to KES 1.2 million. Choose a location with foot traffic: near a market, bus stage, or university. Do a simple count: stand outside for 2 hours and count people passing. Aim for at least 200 adults per hour. Negotiate rent with a 3-month deposit instead of 6. Hire a manager you trust and train them for 3 months in your first salon. Pay them a base salary plus 10% of net profit to motivate. Alternatively, consider franchising. Franchising means someone else uses your brand and systems for a fee. You must have a proven model, a operations manual, and a training program. In South Africa, salon franchises like Sorbet charge R150,000 upfront plus 8% monthly royalty. Start by documenting every process: how to greet clients, mix relaxer, sterilize tools, handle complaints. Then find a franchisee who has salon experience and capital. Provide ongoing support: monthly visits, marketing materials, and bulk buying discounts. Do not franchise if your own salon is not profitable. Both paths require systems, cash, and patience. Test with a pop-up or mobile unit first to reduce risk.

lessons.title: Adding New Service Lines or Products
lessons.body: Adding services increases revenue without moving location. Start by asking your existing clients what they want. Use a simple survey: 'What service would you pay for that we don't offer?' Common additions in African salons: braiding, weaving, manicures, pedicures, facials, makeup, and wig installation. For each new service, calculate startup cost. A basic manicure station needs a table, lamp, tools, and polish: about KES 15,000. You can charge KES 500 per manicure. If you do 5 per day, that's KES 2,500 daily, KES 75,000 monthly. After supplies (KES 10,000) and labor (KES 20,000), you net KES 45,000. That's a 60% margin. For products, start with retail: shampoos, conditioners, oils, and edge control. Buy in bulk from suppliers like Beauty Click in Nigeria or Suzie Beauty in Kenya. Mark up 50-100%. Display near the mirror so clients see them. Train your staff on how to recommend products. A simple script: 'This oil will keep your scalp healthy between visits.' Track sales weekly. If a product doesn't sell in 30 days, replace it. For services, pilot for one month. If less than 10 clients book, drop it. Use WhatsApp to announce new services with before-and-after photos. Offer a 20% discount for the first week. Reinvest profits into marketing. Don't add too many services at onceâmaster one, then add another. This keeps quality high and avoids overwhelming your team.

lessons.title: Partnerships and Collaborations
lessons.body: Partnerships grow your salon without cash. Look for businesses that serve the same clients: photographers, makeup artists, clothing boutiques, wedding planners, and gyms. Approach them with a clear offer. For example, partner with a photographer: you provide hair and makeup for their clients, they give you 15% commission. Or a gym: offer members a 10% discount on services, and the gym promotes you to their list. In Lagos, a salon partnered with a bridal shop and got 20 new clients per month. To find partners, attend local business meetings, use LinkedIn, or simply walk into nearby shops. Prepare a one-page proposal: who you are, what you offer, what you want. Start with a trial period of 3 months. Track results: how many clients came from each partner. Use a simple spreadsheet or notebook. For collaborations, co-host events: a 'pamper party' with a boutique. Split costs and profits 50/50. Promote on Instagram and WhatsApp. Another option: barter. You do hair for a photographer's team, they take professional photos for your portfolio. No money exchanged. Always have a written agreement, even a simple one. Include: services, commission, duration, and exit terms. Review partnerships quarterly. If a partner doesn't bring clients, end it politely. Focus on 2-3 strong partnerships rather than many weak ones. This builds trust and steady referrals.

lessons.title: Scaling Operations and Systems
lessons.body: Scaling means doing more without breaking. Start by documenting every task in your salon. Create a simple operations manual: opening checklist, closing checklist, client intake form, service steps, and cleaning schedule. Use a notebook or Google Docs. For example, a opening checklist: unlock, turn on lights, check appointment book, sanitize tools, count cash float. This lets anyone run the salon. Next, invest in software. Use a booking app like Fresha or Booksy. They are free for basic use and handle appointments, reminders, and payments. In Kenya, M-Pesa integration is key. Set up a till number for easy payments. Track inventory with a simple Excel sheet: product name, quantity, reorder level. When stock hits reorder level, order from supplier. For staff, create clear roles. A receptionist handles bookings and payments. Stylists focus on clients. A cleaner maintains hygiene. Pay based on performance: base salary plus commission on services and product sales. For example, 40% commission on services, 10% on retail. Train staff monthly on new techniques. Use free YouTube videos or bring in a trainer. To scale, you need repeatable processes. Test a new system in your first salon for 2 weeks before rolling out. Measure key numbers: average service time, client wait time, revenue per chair. If a chair makes less than KES 50,000 monthly, optimize or remove it. Consider bulk buying to reduce costs. Join a salon owners' WhatsApp group for supplier deals. Scaling is about systems, not just more chairs.

lessons.title: Franchising Basics for Beauty Businesses
lessons.body: Franchising lets you expand using other people's money and effort. You (franchisor) give a franchisee the right to use your brand, systems, and training in exchange for fees. Before franchising, your salon must be profitable for at least 2 years and have a documented operations manual. You also need a trademark. In Nigeria, register with the Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC). In Kenya, with the Kenya Industrial Property Institute (KIPI). Costs: trademark registration can be KES 20,000 to KES 50,000. Then create a franchise agreement. It should cover: upfront fee, monthly royalty, territory, training, support, and termination. Typical upfront fee for a small salon franchise: $2,000 to $5,000. Royalty: 5-10% of gross sales. You must provide initial training (2-4 weeks) and ongoing support (monthly visits, marketing). Find franchisees through your client base, social media, or franchise expos. Vet them: do they have salon experience? Capital? A good location? For a salon, franchisees need at least $10,000 to $20,000 to open. You earn from upfront fees, royalties, and product sales. But franchising requires legal and accounting help. Budget $1,000 to $3,000 for a lawyer to draft agreements. Also, you must protect your brand: enforce standards. If a franchisee uses cheap products, it hurts you. Do regular audits. Start with one franchisee in a different city. Learn from it. Then expand slowly. Franchising is not passive incomeâit's a new business managing other businesses.

lessons.title: Exit Strategies and Selling Your Salon
lessons.body: Selling your salon is a growth strategyâit lets you cash out and move on. To get a good price, your salon must run without you. Buyers pay for systems, client list, and profit. Start preparing 12 months before selling. Clean up your financials: use a separate bank account, keep receipts, and file taxes. A buyer will ask for 3 years of profit and loss statements. If you don't have them, create them now. Value your salon using a multiple of annual profit. Small salons in Africa typically sell for 1.5 to 3 times annual net profit. If your salon nets KES 1,200,000 per year, you could sell for KES 1.8 to 3.6 million. Also include assets: chairs, dryers, inventory, and your brand. To find buyers, tell your staff, clients, and other salon owners. List on business marketplaces like BizBuySell or local Facebook groups. Or hire a brokerâthey charge 10% commission. Before selling, sign a non-compete agreement: you won't open a similar salon nearby for 2-3 years. Also, train the buyer or their manager for 1 month. If you can't sell, consider closing. Sell assets separately: chairs, mirrors, products. Or pass the salon to a family member. Another exit: merge with a larger salon chain. They might buy your client list. Always get a lawyer to review the sale contract. Don't rush. A rushed sale often gets a low price. Plan your exit at least a year ahead.
